blocks.x: Richard Brunus Your name if you wish.
My name is Richard Brunus. I'm 69 years old.

Could you give us your exact birth date? We'd like to have all that. I'm born in 1889, November 29. Could you tell us a little bit about your father? I don't even know his first name except Mr. Brunus.

Well, my father, he was the leader of our little junior band we had. His name was? And his name was Henry Brunus. Henry, too. Yeah. And he had my sister playing guitar. One of my other brothers playing guitar. He had to wait for him out. My brother Rudy playing guitar. And little Henny had to stand on a chair to play string bass. And I was the only one that didn't play anything. So my dad used to take us around to places on Saturday nights when he got through. He's White Baker. He was a baker. And he brought us over to Mr. Fred Wideman's on Jackson Avenue and the riverfront. And he had a little party over there. And we all went over there and played music. All but me. I was what you call the rosin carrier. So, Mr. Wideman said, well, Henry, what's the matter with the other son? He's the only one that ain't playing. He said, oh, we ain't got no instrument for him. So, next day I passed there. Mr. Wideman called me. He said, Richard, come here. He said, go home and show this to your daddy and I want you to learn it. And he gave me a trumpet, an E-flat trumpet, like things they don't use today. And I took that E-flat trumpet. My grandmother used to live next to a stave yard. And I was on top of them stave piles morning and night, blowing that trumpet. How old were you when you started? About 12 years old. And my grandmother used to holler up there, you loafer, you loafer, get down out of there. So, I kept on going and going. So, I started to pick it up a little bit. So, I played here and then. So, a lot of the bands got to hearing me. So, they come at night. My mother and father would let me go out at night. Did your father help you with the instrument? Did he teach you anything? No, I learnt myself. The stern blazer. Yes. And he used to tell me, no, you got to go to bed. So, I had a little side way to get out at night. And I used to play what you call Freeman's Band. The hoist band I played with. All string. I was the only trumpet player. So, that went on. So, there's other bands. Got to hearing me and all like that. So, they come around the house and ask the old man, could I take a place in the band? So, he said, no, he's too young. He's got to go to school. So, I said, well, on the sideline, I'm going to sneak out again. So, I did so. So, I found I got a little of age. A little of age. I told my father. I said, pa, I'm going to be a musician. You're a baker. And I'm going to be a musician. I said, well, all right, go ahead and do what you want. Well, first thing you know, I was playing in Fisher's Band. Well, could you tell us a little bit about that? Was Johnny Fisher, was it?
His right name was Phillips, but they used to give him that name Fisher. Fisher. He's dead now. Well, it wasn't his real name. No, Phillips.

What sort of a band did he have? He had a brass band. And we used to play at the Crescent Park and Gretna. And they all used to use two and three trumpets for ten men or twelve men brass. I led the band with one trumpet by myself. They called me what they called the Iron Lick Conniprass. And we used to get on the levee in front of the park, and they used to hear me blow way back on St. Charles Avenue when we were playing music.
People told me when you played on Canal Street, they could hear you over and out.
So that went on, and so I went with Shillen's band. Shillen got a band.
A little bit more about Fisher's Band. What kind of music did they play? Marches or Ragtime? All Ragtime. Ragtime. Can you remember some of the pieces they played? Oh.
I couldn't remember that.
Were the pieces, any of the numbers, like, say, Tiger Rag? Tiger Rag. Yeah, those kind. The Tiger Rag.

And the tin roof blues. Bucket's got a hole in it. What was number? And, uh... Dixeland One Step? Huh? Dixeland One Step? Dixeland One Step. And, uh, old gray bonnet. Dixeland One Tip stuff like a little dance, a little party. And we used to go. And like me, I used to play out at different places at night, all night, Saturday night, get up Sunday morning, go play all day picnic at Millen Boyd. And from Millen Boyd, we'd go to Crescent Park or Bacong Grove, and I'd keep blowing up. Bacong Grove was over in Gretna. Yeah, and I used to keep up there.

I used to get up the next morning and go to work in the brook. Well, about where was that pecan grove? I've heard about it. I don't know. It's up there in Crescent Park. I know where the ferry was. Between Harvey and Gretna. Up in there. Is it right on the river? Right on the river, yes. Is there anything left there now? No. Nothing in all the Goplin's Hall.

And they used to have a Finan's Hall up there. I used to play in that too. I used to play in the fish's band. And the Crockett's Hall in Gretna. Jack Lane. And Owl's Hall. And the Owl's Hall. And uh... Tell them about the Emmett Hardy.
Well, yeah, but tell us about Emmett Hardy. Did you know him when he was starting out on drumming?

Yeah, Emmett Hardy was a good little jazz connet player. So, he used to come up and he used to follow me all over and try to get ideas and all like that for me. And he went out and he went out wonderful. And it's a pity that he had to die so young. He did, yeah. He did, yeah. He did, yeah. He did, yeah. And, uh... Roger. And the Hardy. And the Hardy, yeah. That was it. And Dick, what about the carnival balls?
It's alright, Mrs. Brunish, if you want to say something, dude, you can move up there and you don't have to play.

We used to play at the Outfellas Hall, big balls like the Druids, Masons and all like that, the Fishies Band, you know. Did they play parades too, like carnival? Parades, yeah. Like carnival parades, we used to have five, uh, five, uh, the whole five carnival parades. The other time I was one trumpet player with two bands. And the floats, they used to be led by mules.
Yeah, I remember some of them.

And they used to be slow. So, one of their bands short a trumpet player. No, no trumpet player. So, I used to take one band, start it off. When I get through, I run up, up to the other band, start that band off, and they go to town. And when they stop, I'll drop back to the other band. And I've been doing that for many years. So, I got just over.
What kind of music did they play in the parades then?

Marches and, uh, ragtime marches. They started jazzed them up then too in ragtime. Yeah, that's right. They call them ragtime. No jazz them days. Yes, it's ragtime. And if everybody ceased to love, put that in it.
They always played that too then.
Locked East. And, uh, pled funerals. Pled funerals with Jack Lane.
Where did they have those, uh, what, uh, the funerals? Did you march to the graveyard? Yeah, right to the graveyard. Mm-hmm.
They used to blow the taps. They wanted to bear it up. You know. So the clock, you see.

And, uh, yes. I wondered about coming back, uh, on the way to the funeral, did you play just funeral marches? No, did you ramble? On the way back then you played, didn't he ramble? Jazz music. How far back was that when you had those funerals? Do you remember about how early, how old you were, or when the year would be? I must have been about, 21. You were 21. Yeah. Was that with Papa Jack Lane's band?

No, this was Fish's band. Fish's band played the funerals too. And I played the funerals with Jack too. Jack used to have him on the counter. He was a prophet, you see. He belonged to the prophet. Yeah. Well, there was only one man in the city. How long was that? He had a larger funeral and Grandpa Henry Burman. That was Mayor Martin Burman. Is that right? And that's we, Fisher, and he's there and played for Mayor Burman's daughter when she made her communion over in Algea. That's when he was living. Yes. And he had a hot band over there. That was four Algea's of Spade and stuff. They had new cars and all. Mm-hmm. And, yeah.

That was so long. Well, see, I can think of a few things to ask. I was gonna ask, when you first played with Papa Lane, did you play in his Reliance band, or what was it called? Well, it was the Reliance band.
He called it the Reliance band, yes. Reliance. And I called it Jack, Jack Lane. Yes.
Somebody told me he had more than one band.
Yeah, he had a couple bands, yeah. They called it Babies or something, wasn't it? Huh? Was it Papa Lane, these Babies or something like that? Name, that's all I know when he was right down there.
Was he always, he didn't play in all of them, of course, if he had more than one band, did he send somebody else out as leader, or did he appoint? Yeah, he'd go higher, higher, you see.

He had some Reliance that played music, like Bill Gowesley, Lawrence Vega, he's dead, trumpet player. His son played, too. And Chink Martin. Yes, I know Chink, he's still alive. And Pangelline, his son, used to play trumpet. And between him and they had about two bands, two or three bands, his Reliance.
What did the bands pay in those days? How much money would you make for a parade?
Oh, well then they'd down and a half all night.
Really?
Some of them five dollars. Eight or two.

How could a parade pay? Parade, parade, five thousand, man. The big carnival parades, too. Yeah. You mentioned about the five organizations, which were those, Rex and Momus and... All of them, the whole five of them were played.
Well, the Coles. Was Rex, Momus, Comus, Proteus? I can't think of the other ones. But those are the four oldest clubs. Those are the prominent fathers. Yes.
I wondered what the five were, yeah. Anyway, those are the main ones. Rex, Comus, Momus, and Proteus. That's it. So those are the big ones today.

Yeah, then I used to go out to Millen Boyd and blow the roofs off the... There's all tin roofs out there. And I'd get up there with fishing and shilling, sometime with Jacqueline. Well, shilling's different, isn't it? Yeah, shilling is still... I talked to him one day. Yeah. And we'd go out there in the morning, with white suits on, and come back with our white suits loaded with cinders. Oh, yeah. From Smokey Murray. And not only our pockets loaded with cinders, something else, too, you know. So, we all used to have a good time, and all used to say, well, where's Rich yet? He ain't in the band. Well, he said, you know, the band would strike up. I'd leave one in the band, a leader. Put him next to what I'm gonna do. You know, these big attics in them places out there with cross pieces and all like that. So, they played, different albums all like that, and all of a sudden it stopped. And I picked it up. And there was one way that... The trouble it was coming from when I was way up in the attic. That would be a dance band, would it? How big a band did you use? About 76, 79, 70. And, I'm telling you, one man just played two drums, you know.

Yes, the bass drum with the flip pedal. Yeah. And, uh, we also... I was gonna ask about some of the other bands, the real old time bands. For instance, Emil Tasso's band, Spanish Fork. Did you ever hear that? Who? Tasso? Tasso. What kind of a band was that? That was Tasso, a big concert band. Did you ever play in that? No, no, no. That was all music they used there, yes. All music. Played by music. Was that a pretty big band? How big was it? About 20 men. 20 men. Yeah, sometimes more. How late did they play? About 11 o'clock. I mean, in years. When did they play as late as the First World War? Or when and how long did they play?

Oh, yeah. Before the First World War. Oh, yeah. Before the First World War. Before the First World War. Before the... I had a little stunt coming up. About the 1908's, huh? Grandma and I used to... His mother, I used to take... I was a walking stick. I used to take... She used to take me all around. I'd take all around. Oh, no. What else do you want?
There's another military band. Was it Brown's? Red Brown, yeah.
He's dead.
Well, there's Tom Brown. Tom Brown. Is he living yet? No, he's dead. He's dead, too, yeah. He just died a year ago.
I never did play with him. We never did play with Tom Brown. We were fighting against one of them. A little bit late, a hot stuff. Yeah. So we outgrew them. And... Not a bad thing.
Do you remember the Detroit brothers? Detroit, yeah. Detroit, yeah.
Detroit, yeah.

Did you ever play with them? No. Johnny played Trump. Johnny played Trump. Johnny played Trump. I took a couple lessons from Johnny, but I didn't like it. I figured it would come out of my head. He was better than sitting down with music. Yeah. Yeah. He's one of our old neighbors, Johnny Deetra. Yeah, Johnny Deetra. Is that right? That's right. Wonderful people. An old man used to tell me, you're going to regret it. You're going to regret it. I said, no, I ain't. I said, what comes out that head is good, and it's good and hot. I said, ain't no marches. Richie, what was the name of the old fella? I worked out for Grover, and he played. He was trying to give me trombone lessons. He worked for Grover out there. He was an old trombone player. Oh, Ricky Tom? Ricky Tom. He told me. Rock hitters, you never learn how to read a note. Then I used to play out at Anderson. I was a white trumpet player. I didn't play either. In Anderson. It was Louis Armstrong playing that first. George is the one that. Tom Anderson at the Rampart and Canal.
Yes, near Canal.

So it was Grover, his wife, his brother-in-law, and Ricky Tomes, and myself, and August Shillain. He's there, three, three, three, not so long ago. And we used to play at Anderson. Some Anderson. And they did away with Armstrong. Armstrong went up north and did good. Yeah. And I stayed down there and did bad.
Oh, well, maybe you had a good time, too, here.
I think my family was too big and I didn't want to travel.
I was going to ask about some of the other old-time cornet players that maybe you worked with or got to hear, like Manuel Mello.
Manuel, yeah. That's Lane's son-in-law. Old man Lane.
Was he older than you?
No, about the same age. About the same age. He's a lion. Works on the poles. He used to do it. He used to play trumpet, too.

And Lawrence Vega. Lawrence Vega. Is he older than you or about the same age? Oh, he's older. Older man than you. He's dead, too. He was hot, too. Is he a good hot trumpet player that played ragtime? Oh, yeah.
How about your friend on Constant Street, the Italian man that was... Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah. How did he play in the old days?

He was an uncle. Really? To me, he was in my time. We used to play up at Beznor's. Had a band up at Beznor's. And before he had to do a trumpet. We used to play up at Olderwise, dancing school. Olderwise. And he used to come up there. And when I was going to take intermission, go out and sit down in my chair and take my trumpet and pull with it like that. All of a sudden, he was like, I don't know how to play it. He did good, too. Oh, yeah. I see. He fusses. He said he writes articles and I think he misses all of all the jazz.
Yes, I know. He sometimes claims that he originated all of the jazz. Oh, I know.

That's ridiculous. I'll tell you who originated jazz. It was Georgia Burns, Leo Rapola, Rag Baby Stevens, and Chink. Yeah, I believe it was Chink, Chink, Chink. And I don't know who was the other two. There were two more in the band. And them's the one who originated jazz. Some of the New Orleans rhythm gigs. New Orleans rhythm. Paul Moreau. Yeah. Paul Moreau. Yeah, Paul Moreau. Yeah, that's right. It was Paul Moreau's, too. Yeah. And them's the boys that originated jazz here. Went up north and did good. When they went up north, musicians up there didn't know what to make of the music. So they got the hang of it, and they're playing it now today. Well, you see, Lawrence Welk plays. He always has one of his sidelines there, the Dixage band. Yes, that's right. You see, Bill, there was a difference in the type of music that Nick LaRocca played and the type of music that Georgie and Paul Moreau's and rap. In other words, they really dressed it up.
Yeah.
They played ragtime music. We played jazz.
You mean Nick LaRocca and his bunch. Played ragtime.

No, ragtime. We slept in the niggas. The niggas, they don't play no jazz. They don't play jazz. There was then five men that originated jazz. They really, they really. Now, the whole other. Rap Polar, George Applernish, and Rag Baby Stevens. He's there. And Rap Polar's there, too. And Paul Moreau's there, too. And Paul Moreau. Yeah, that's right. And Chink Martin. And bass.
There are a couple of other trumpet players. I was going to ask some names I don't know about. George Barth. Do you remember? Oh, Barth.
Yeah, he used to play a piece of two sometimes.
He played? Yeah. Was he a fairly old man? Is he older than you? No, he's about my age. About your age.
He's dead, isn't he?
I think so. I don't know about him.

He used to go on the love of Paul Young Abner. And he used to play with fish sometimes, you know. Sometimes when I couldn't make it, why, he went and played with fish. You remember Harry Shannon. Harry Shannon, yeah. He was an umpore player. He was an umpore player.
What do you mean by that? He wasn't very good? He wasn't good at all.
Oh, we know Harry. He was raised. Yeah, Harry Shannon. You're on Little Jackson. He played a, well, a straight. Yeah, just a straight. Like in church. Yeah. Good church.
Freddie Newrock. Do you remember?
Yeah, I know Freddie. Newrock, is it? Freddie Newrock. Yeah, he played in all these big brass bands. Seems like it. But all about music. He played by music. He couldn't fake a note.

Another name I have here is Pete Dietrich. Do you remember that? Pete Dietrich. Pete, it looks like Dietrich. No, I don't remember. Is that a white man? Yes, I think so. And Doc looks like Berriesen. B-E-H. Orange? Orange? No, B-E. B-E-H-R-E-A-S-O-N. Barenzy? Barenzy? Barenzy? Barenzy? Maybe that's it. Barenzy? No, I don't know. Doc? I don't know. Yeah. No, I don't know yet. Those are some of the names I was going to ask you about. And what about the Christian boys? Do you remember them? All of them. Yeah. All Frank Christian, Charlie Christian, Johnny Christian.
Emil?
Emil. Emil, he's still around. He is. He's still playing bass with them, isn't he? Yes, he plays bass. He still plays his trombone sometimes. Yeah, yeah. Double's on.

No, I don't know. Double. Down the corner. Brookhaven. I know all of Brookhaven. Can any of them down? No, I don't. That's probably it. That's it there. Might be not from Brookhaven. Brookhaven, yeah. Yeah. Might be there. They used to have a big brass band, too. I don't know if they played with them. Richard, do you remember old man Mendelson that used to play piano from the neighborhood? His son's playing with the Dukes of Dixieland now. Yeah, Stanley Mendelson. The boy. Mendelson. Huh? Mendelson. Well, his daddy was really more of a good, I mean, a note man. Was he an organist? I think he was. He was an organist. Yeah. I don't think Dick knows him.

He was from the neighborhood originally. I was going to ask about Joe Lala, too. Did he have a band? Yeah, he had a band. He was pretty cool in the right town. And... And... They had two brothers. Yes, Johnny... Johnny and... Johnny.
And the Majada boys. Sala Majada.
Sala Majada. I played with them. One boy plays clarinet. He's living in. He's living in. He's living in.

Johnny, he died not so long ago. And Vincent? And Vincent. Vincent was married to... Vincent don't play. Who was the one who played the clarinet? Johnny. Johnny. He's the one who married to... Teresa Gates. Gates, I mean. Living on Phillips Street. He married everyone from across the river. No, but his first wife was Teresa Gates. Gates. My mother's cousin. Living on Phillips Street.

That's all right. I'm glad to have all those things. He wants all that. Yes, all this information that we can find is fine. I'm going to ask about Johnny Stein, the drummer. Johnny Stein. If he had a band here, if he was one of the old timers or...
He played at the Alamo Theater. I remember him when a woman shot his ear off.
Oh, really?
Oh, my. He shot his ear off. I put it in here. Yeah. He was a wonderful fellow drummer. And he had all the women.

How did he? Did you ever play with him much? No, I didn't play with him, no. And Bill Gallaty, did you mention you played with him? Yeah, I played with Bill Gallaty. Did he have his own band? No, he played with Lane and different bands, you know. And Joe Baraka.
Baraka.
Joe Baraka. I don't know.
I didn't play with him.
You didn't play with him. Do you remember the Gallagher band?
Bill Gallaty? Yeah, I know. He's a triangle player, too. But I never really played. He didn't have a band. He played with different bands. With different bands.

I was going to ask a little bit more about your family. You say your grandfather gave your father this violin that we have. I think so. He came from your grandfather. Yeah, I think it comes from all...
He came from all sales for rain.
He came from over in the old country.
Yeah, when Frank said, that's what his father, your grandfather, I was just that. All sales for rain. Under the French flag.
Yes, under the French.

That's how it's working. Brunis. B-R-U-N-I-S. Whatever we'd write to the relatives in Germany, we always had to address it B-R-U-N-I-A-S. Because I remember... Well, they were German. Yeah. But they were under a French flag. Under the French flag. And also... How the E got in there? Well, I'm not. But the original family name was I-A-S. Because we had an aunt. I remember. We had a translator. Translate a letter. Her name was Data. D-A-T-A. I remember that as plain as I can see it now. And Grandma had some German come over. And interpret her, you see. And interpret her the letter. And was telling us... It was after World War I. Telling us what a condition that World War I had left them. Oh, yes. That was terrible. And they were pretty wealthy people before the war. One of the sons of this aunt Data was a very prominent engineer. And he was killed in World War I. In fact, they owned a hotel in Burlum. I mean, that's what the contents of the weather was. And another thing I want to say. I guess you all remember the Palisade. He used to put on all that vulnerable stuff.
Yes, I've heard of it. That was before my time.

Well, I was down there. I wasn't so old. I wasn't so young. I was there one time and I seen a girl, a young girl come out playing two trumpets at one time. Oh, yeah. And I do. I go along the line, Port Street, and I find me another trumpet. And one or two at a time, I was playing two trumpets. Oh, two at a time. Yeah, two at a time. I had kilometers. He used to go on plays. I always lived, please.

Oh, yeah. When did you give up music? How long since you played music? I thought about 20 years ago. 25 years. 25 years. 25 years. You have a better memory than any of us. Well, it was a happy day in my life. Oh, who tell it? Did you ever have your own band that you were the leader that just played with other bands?

Well, you had the band when you was out in Bucktown. It was your band. Oh, I took it. I was Jesus in the band. Yeah, but I mean, it was still your band. East End. East End. East End. East End. Uncle Lemon. Didn't like the name of Bucktown, so they had a change. No. East End. East End. East End. East End. East End. East End. Violin. Not me. Violin, the piano. Buck Rogers. And drum. Buck Rogers. Me on trumpet. And a banjo player. And it wasn't that far from the roof garden. And that roof garden band was sentimental, you know. They had owls up there. Oh, sometimes. You remember that, yeah? You're making me up now. Yeah. And they all used to play music. And I used to throw that trumpet over towards them, you know. It was high. High they were. And some of them just say, that damn fellow would take that trumpet and throw it away. We don't know where we are on the music. You're not supposed to play. They only sent a word over there about me not playing so loud and everything like that, so I had to cut it down.
Who was playing over at the roof garden? Uh, what's his name? You like?
And? Who's similar?
No.

Was Sharky ever over there? No, it was Correct. Yeah, he was a doctor. Medanovich. Pinky. Oh, the boy. Pinky. Pinky. Pinky. Medanovich. Yeah, the doctor. Medanovich. The Owls. Yeah, the Owls. The Owls. Yeah. And I used to blow the roof. Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah. You really learned by yourself, and you didn't have any lessons except a couple you learned.

And the reason the other boys learned, I went out and bought the instruments and I couldn't blow them like a trombone. Trombone? They were on the yard or laid on the table. Mm-hmm. Older's brother Henney come along, he picked it up. He learned it. Well, he's dead now.

Well, can you tell us a little bit about your brother, Henry, because he's not here, of course, to talk for us. Well, he was a hot friend. He was a wonderful, I've heard. Yes, he was. He was a showman with his son. I had that to say. How much younger was he than you? He was younger than you? Oh, yeah. Next to him. About five years. About five years. And, uh...

He'd be about 65. What's his name? Merritt and them, they did the same thing. I'd buy an instrument, they'd come along behind me and pick it up and blend it up. That's how they all went out. I'd blow a blow and essence.

How much older was Rudy than you? About... Oh, Rudy was about three or four. About five years. About five years old. Oh, you're 69? He'd be... Yeah, about five. That's right. That's right. I'm right. How old was your father when he died? Do you remember? 62, I believe. And when was that? Oh, I spent quite some time. About 10, quite some time. About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10... About 10...
Did your father ever play professionally, ever work in a band or anything except your own little band?
It was wonderful to hear that we had a store, my father did, my mother, right opposite. Am I interfering?
No, that's fine. I'm glad to have you.

And right opposite on Jackson Avenue in Russo. And they lived across the opposite side, a little bit farther down. And he used to have them all up on the porch, the front porch. And I'll tell you, it was just wonderful to hear that band in the evening, you know, play on. And then we had the river right there with those ships playing the, what do you call it? Aquarians. Aquarians, you see. But this band, his father really entertained the whole neighborhood with those children playing.
And then that violin boy broke over our head. We didn't do it right while he swung that violin boy.
Well, my shit, he's one of those.
That's all right. That's funny. What kind of music did you play? Remember some of the pieces? Were they ragtime or waltzes? Oh, it was straight music and all.

And the lances, more of the lances, the varieties and shardish waltzes, you know. Especially that malkin boy on that E string, you know. We had to be quiet when we played that malkin boy on that bullish church, you know, on that string. You had to keep quiet. You had to be quiet.
My father was a real minstrel, that's true. That was a big dungy. Every morning, every morning, I opened the stove. He came out to get his little nip.

I was going to ask about other music. The very first music you remember hearing when you were a boy. Do you remember what kind of music? Did you hear any music down at the river? Or was it parades? Or your father playing? Or what was the first music?
I imagine you copied plenty of that off those folks. Oh, parades.

Like my daddy used to have a big phonograph, you know. It was a cylinder ring. Oh, yes. And we had a bar on my people. Yeah, bar on the confectionery. And I used to have my trumpet underneath the ball all the time. New piece come out, I put it on, I line it. And I played that day, that night at a ball or a picnic, I got the rest of the fellas to play it. And the whole band of players, I know people. I used to say, how are you learning pieces so quick? I said, it comes through my head.
It's nice to have this. We remember it all the time. We had this on the record.
You remember them all the time.

You were going to talk about your father a little bit being a fine violin player. Oh, yeah. He was a nice father. Not fine music. Just all my ear. Yes. Did he ever have any lessons, do you think? Or did his father help him? Where did he learn it? Did he ever say? I don't know. He just picked it up. He just picked it up. He just picked it up. He just picked it up. He just picked it up. He just picked it up. Yep. Where was your house where you lived? Jackson Avenue, Chapel Tula.
Chapel Tula. And...
2119 Chapel Tula. Chapel Tula. That's where I was born. They're there too. In the same old house. Same old house.
That's right.
And that balcony where they played, was that upstairs? Up high? Upstairs. Upstairs. And they played up high, didn't they?

Yes. A front balcony. I'll tell you, they entertained the whole neighborhood. And they were wonderful boys. Never got into trouble. Only among themselves. Never had arguments. If they did, it was indoors. But those children never caused any sorrow to that mother and father. That's a wonderful record for all boys. Yes. Just one girl, unless you married early.
Was that called the Irish Channel? Oh, we were in the middle of the Irish Channel.
I hate to say that, because all my children were raised there. I'm proud of it. I'm proud of it myself. But we... Oh, Lord.
There were a lot of good people. That's right. A lot of good. Self-made people. We were in the Jackson Avenue, you see.
But they lived the block out further.
We lived closer to the river.
Yes.
The boats were right there close to you. Yes. They were closer. Closer than they are now.

It was better. That was a poor man. The river was a poor man's west end. Because west end, they had to go out there in a trolley. And you had to pay toll to go out there. Yes. At Metairie. There was a lady, Miss Murphy. She was a toll keeper. And she, you had to pay her, I don't know whether it was two minutes, 15 cents, something like that, to go through. But we used to go in on the trolley. And the child would go out to West End. He used to lose his band. See, it was way out in the air, out in the water. Oh, yes. And then they used to get a table set where you take them. See, marvelous. But I want to tell you, the river was a poor man's west end. And everybody could have bought it. I was out there.

The kids go in swimming down there? Well, I mean, you take on a Sunday afternoon. Yes. All the families go out on the riverfront. And there was one girl named Bebe Harrison. She used to jump, I mean, dive off the shed. Run and dive off the top of the shed.
Into the river. Into the river. And then, you know, they had the back shore. And it used to go walk down, you see. And, of course, that's how all of those children were drowned, too.
I learned something I want to tell you. Oh, yes. Excuse me. All right. Certainly. My daddy was a patron. Yes. And they used to sell pious under the river. And they used to have a whole fusil.
Oh, really?

And they had a little horse, blind horse. The horse was blind. And they had a little four-wheel wagon. And they used to go all along the riverfront, along that bugle. And you'd see long showmen, scroamers, and all kinds of different kinds of ways to buy the pies. See? So, when he winded up, the old man, his name was Pick. Pick, I don't know, down on the riverfront. He kept a saloon.
Another one.
And by the time he got down there, he was sold out of part. But that blind horse had to bring him home.
Another set.

And they got two playing, he used to play banjo, too, those men. Him and Pick. I called Pick, that's what I called him. And that blind horse had come along from the gate wasn't open on Chappatula Street. He fought like that. The old grandma Burnett's car. Damn it to hell, Hiney's drunk again. This is awesome. All the pies sold out in the back of the way. Oh, I don't know exactly.
That's all right. No, that's all right. We have all sorts of things on. That's all right.
No, you won't hear my background. That's why I'm trying to get them.

That's all right. We have some awfully funny stuff goes on this tape sometimes. Some people get talking. So that's nothing at all. I was going to ask about that baker shop. Did you live right above that or was it in the same building? Same building. It was on the first floor.

It was a perfectionary and a bar room. Because the sailors, and they used to come in there, were right on the river. They were right on the river. Yes. You see, they used to have horse cars there. Then later on they had electric cars. But it was mostly horse cars when they lived there. You see, because when it commenced to go down, then they moved farther in on Jackson Avenue. The neighborhood went down. And the grandmother died. So then they just kept moving in. Moved further into Jackson Avenue. Got more sedate.
Because you lived on Rousseau and Jackson.
I lived on Jackson and Rousseau. Jackson and Rousseau. Right next to the engine house.
That was a good neighborhood. As I say, the Irish Channel was supposed to be sort of rough. But everybody in that neighborhood tried to help each other.

But you see, my father had a business there. You know, a big place too. It was 110 front by 180 steps. Oh, Lord. The building's still there. Yeah. Still there. Yeah, but there's no porches or nothing. It's just like everything else. It's like French port. If it wasn't kept up, it'd be that high. Mm-hmm.

Yes. Yeah, I used to take fishing's band with one trumpet with 10, 12 men. On Mardi Gras Day, early in the morning, 9 o'clock. One time, 8 o'clock. From the Slot House up to the Audubon Park. Oh, and around Canal Street. All in and out different places. People's home. That's the time we used to have kegs of beer at people's homes. Where is it? And donuts and all. Hot weenies. And I'd be going all that day. This was one trumpet.
One coronet. I suppose you played coronet in those days rather than a trumpet, right? Yeah, it was a coronet.
The one I liked always about that small was the E-flat trumpet.
A little short E-flat you started with?
Yeah. And I found out I had a bigger one.
What make did you like? What was your favorite coronet?
A king, I used to have a king.

King. Now tell me, when you used the E-flat, did you play a different part than the regular B-flat part? Octave high and any other instrument. Octave high, yeah. Did you just stick to the lead or did you play some fancy runs like the clarinet part?

That's right. You can do that too. Stick to the fancy too. Mm-hmm. Well, you best carry a straight lead. Carry a straight lead with it, you see. And that helps the rest of the band out. Sure. You used to have a variation in the band, the rest of the band. I don't know what the devil is all about.
Sure, that's right.
Yeah, they... You've got to have a straight lead.
For the rest of the band to catch in on them. Yeah. You mentioned the slaughterhouse. Where was that? That's where they kill all the beef. Down in St. Canale. In Araby. In Araby. Way down there.
Yeah. Well, it's that way down. It's far enough, but it's... It's about the 1,600 blocks. About 1,600. 1,600 below Canale's there. It's about 1,600. 800, 1,700.
About Brother Canale is the... Oh, yeah.
It's called the Crescent City Club. It used to play for the Garden Districts. Fish and...
They went from one end of the world to do it.
Yeah, all that in one day, March all day.
And I remember his brother...
Five dollars for that day.

Yeah. Five dollars. I remember his brother, Abby. With the beer and stuff, we used to do. Mr. Russell. His brother, Abby, used to get on... He used to play in these clubs, I think. And he used to play... And his wife worked in the... In the five and ten cents store or something. And he's just... All night, he'd be playing that piece. I said, I've... I won my wife in the five and ten cents store. And I tell you, everybody knew it was Abby on that end. He played to his girlfriend in the five and ten cents store.

I don't know if Abby ever told you about... How you used to jam the silk paintings up in there. No, I don't believe so. They had a place on Common Street, right off the dryings. In the speaking easy days. Called a Hotsi Totsi. And the racehorse men used to go up in there. And Abby, Jan, that silk paintings. Who was one of the grandpas's henkerchiefs. And the bell of the horn. And it would sound like it was maybe ten miles away. You know, it was... It would be pretty. And they threw a hundred dollar bills in the kid. Fifty dollar bills. Take the kid and bust it up that night. Nose lock it. I'll turn on... This is Richie talking.
Yeah.

This ain't Henny Bernis, you know. His wife. Another thing, I could take a cornet and turn it into a slide trombone. Imitate it. You didn't? Yeah. But did you slide the... No, I just play all the pedal notes and change my slides. Oh.
I thought maybe you'd slide the tuning slide.
Pedal note tone. Yeah. You see? Like a transfer of notes or anything.
Way down a lot of people.

And they all used to come in the place and say, Where's the trombone play at? I said, I did. Trombone. They used. He plays trumpet. I don't believe it. I said, all right, let's go band. Man, you play better trombone play. Pedal notes and all like that. Yeah. Yeah. We used to do good there. We used to do good. We used to do shamrock in them places. You know, doing prohibition.
Where were they located those clubs?
D'Angelo Street. All along D'Angelo Street. Johnny's Place and the shamrock and the sweet potato ring. You go in there already, but I don't know how you're going to come out.
It's called Madison.
I played there before. Did you play the Cadillac? It was on. I played St. Louis on. I got a ramp.

And Abby and Abby. Yeah, Abby was at the Cadillac. Later, the silver slipper of the... Silver slipper, too. I was going to ask one more question about the brass bands. What the lineup was. Like you say, sometime you were the only carnet. How many trombones? What else did they have? Altos, clarinets? Two trombones, tuba, two altos, bass drum, snare drum, two clarinets.
Sometimes two or three French horns.
French horns. Yeah. Would it be real French horns or like the alto, melaphone? Yeah. That go around in a circle. Yeah. The clarinets, did they have E-flat or B-flat?
Some of them had B-flat. Some of them had E-flat. First, second, and third. I imagine them. First, second, and third, fourth, trumpet, crack, trumpet. I used to blow all that out at one time.
When you played with those bands like Fishers or Pop Elaine, did you have any music ever? The other fellas, did they use music? No, no. Just all but him. All but him. Super.
I read it.
Yes, go ahead, Mrs.

I read an editorial one time about George. When he was up north, and the lights went out or something happened, the electricity, I don't know what. And he was the only man who could play because he was playing by ear. He was the only one who could play, all the rest of them. Had no lights, but he kept playing. You know, the comic book.

Did George ever tell you about the time when he was married at Jimmy Ryan's in New York in 52nd? I remember. He wasn't doing any business. He had just started the place, you see. So he takes the band out of the place. All along with the 2nd Street, playing a dog time strutters ball. He's playing the jail.
Hit the front pages of the Daily Noon. They still do that sometimes.
He was the All-American trombone listener.
That's right. He's wonderful.
Well, I'm sorry. I can't have that book. It's a dial-up. It was Esquire, wasn't it?
Esquire. Oh, the Esquire book. That's right. I remember. I've seen that.
Some years back. And he was the All-American. He claimed to be the All-American trombone listener.
Then I played the Mobile. Oh, yes. They called it the Baby of Jazzes. And there were stuff with
Was Henry in that band with you at that time or who else? No. He played over there too, I know, sometimes.
Yeah, I played at the house.
Which band was that you played with? Grover's.
Grover's. Grover, yeah.
Have you met Grover? No, I don't know him with that name. He's out in the air.
What? He's dead. Grover's dead. Oh, yeah.
No, I don't know him. His wife is dead.
Maybe we can talk to her sometime. She played saxophone. I don't know if she plays in the most power. Oh, yeah, alto saxophone. Yes.
I believe she's... What was his full name, Grover? That was his last name? Shepard. Shepard. Shepard.
Shepard.
Shepard. Something like that.
He's got a Sunday out there. Yeah. And I believe she's a bookkeeper for... This one is still on Rampo Street. What? Cushman's.
Cushman's.
Joyce? No. Closy Canouse Street? Cushman's. Closy Canouse Street? Yeah.
Oh, no. The Cushman's way down.

Well, the Cushman's way down. The Duffin's. She's a bookkeeper or something like that. Last time I asked him. She don't know. Oh, no. I know. I know. I know. It's down around the auditorium. Yeah. I can't think of any.
Gold Room.
Gold Room. That's the way. Gold Room. I guess it's Cushman's, that's it.
Well, Cushman's way down on Duffin.
Yeah, that's the way it is.
Well, we can check and see.
Well, someday I'd like to meet her, too.
Yes. She might have some nice information for us.
She was a good saxophone player, but just by music. Not by air. She had a fallout. And then towards that, we called her the Bucktonians. From Bucktown.
Oh, yeah.

And we share, we didn't have, how was it, Stump? We had drums, vocalizers. And, uh, oh, I can't think of anything. He's driving on banjo. I don't know even. And a fellow by the name of Big Boy. And a piano. Girl goes on piano. And we used to have a big bus. I used to travel from one place to the other. Especially when the colleges, the schools, you see. You get in front of a drugstore, pull out a piano, a piece and stuff, a plane, and it's all those girls coming from different places, you know. And, uh, we'd throw a sign up on the drugstore when the world was going to play out the night and they would pack them in like that.

Did you ever use piano much in the early bands? Oh, yeah. I had a piano a lot of times. Yeah. Well, I don't want to bother you anymore. We've been having a nice talk here. I don't want to keep asking you a lot of questions. I can't think of much more. I can't think of much more, actually, to ask you. I wondered if there was any more about the early music, the very first that you heard the kind of parades, even when you were a boy, before you learned to play. Did they have the parades?
Oh, yeah.
Carnival Parades. Did they ever play any ragtime in those days? No, just marches. Just plain marches.
Plain marches.
Mm-hmm.
And had a father behind ewes, didn't they?
Mm-hmm.
The ewes used to pull the floats. Yes. And, uh, Irish bands, brass bands, marches. Yes.

And the very early dance music, when you were a little boy, even before you learned to dance or before you learned to play, can you remember any of the dance music you might have heard from outside of a ballroom or outside of a tavern, what kind of music they might have had?
No, it is from that record, from the phonographs. From the phonographs. Very early. It hit my head like that. Yeah. I'll play that.
And you knew it right away and you could play it right as soon as you heard it.
The beautiful music on the streets. Yeah. On the riverfront. Yeah.
What kind of music was on the riverfront?
Well, it just, it just, just like you see those men playing now, they have a band that comes on now. What is that band? The Polish band that comes on?
Oh. On Charlie and Gene.
Huh? It, I can't call it our band. But, uh, they play exactly like that riverfront.
Those are fine musicians.
That, that Polish band, it comes on Channel 13.
Oh.
Oh.
I can't remember.
They used all the different instruments then, did they? They used cardines. Cardines. Cardines.
Cardines.

But, uh, planets and banjos. They weren't educated men, most of them, but they, it was beautiful. There'd be one ship on top of the other there, you know, docked. And they played beautiful music. It was just as good as going to a, to a concert.
It would be the sailors that came in.

Sailors and the Norwegians and Danes. All the foreigners. All the foreigners, you know, but beautiful music. Beautiful. Really beautiful music. And then, of course, we had the Brunus band entertain us too, you know. Oh, sure. So we really didn't have to go too far, did we? How often? Because all you had was the Nickelodeums in those days, you know. You didn't have the nice plays.
How often did the Brunus band play there on the balcony?
Whenever the father wanted them to.

About once a week. About a couple of whiskers in them, and he had it all over. It would be about every once a week or two or three times a week? Every time I saw him pulling that fiddle, he, shh, shh, that whistle. He's whistling and all the boys come running. Yeah.
They're a good family.
Yes, they must have been.
Yes, you are. Let's see if I was a neighbor next to him, it would have been a noisy family.

Well, I want to thank you for the wonderful visit we've had here. I wish I could tell you more about it. No, that's very good. I think back more. That's very good. I think we have most of that life now down here that we remember about it. And I appreciated hearing about your father too.
Yeah.
And the old times. I'll turn it off. Good stuff. Thank you.
